content:
The Quran makes a public challenge: "If you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah the like thereof" (2:23). A recent post on social media declares the matter closed. "The Quran is not miraculous," it says, because al-Ma'arri's al-Fusul wa al-Ghayat "already fulfilled the quranic challenge", and The True Furqan is "the Christian response", written by Christians and "not just a random Persian".

The claim names two real books, and both have been put forward before. This article aims to provide context to the claim, insha'Allah, in seven answers: what the challenge asks, who al-Ma'arri was, what his book is, who said he meant it as a rival, what he said of it himself, what The True Furqan is, and what follows.

The challenge is repeated in several forms. "Produce a surah like it" (10:38). "Produce ten surahs like it, invented" (11:13).

"If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like" (17:88). "Let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful" (52:34).[1]

Each form asks for a composition that stands beside the Quran, in its own language, in the judgement of those who know that language. The first people to hear the challenge were the poets and orators of Mecca, and the Quran records their answers: they called it poetry, magic and "tales of the ancients" (21:5; 74:24; 25:5).[1]

The early commentators also read the words "like it" as covering what the Quran says as well as how it says it. Al-Tabari records Qatada's gloss: "like this Quran in truth and truthfulness, with no falsehood or lie in it". He records Mujahid's, "like the Quran", and explains the challenge to the Arabs as a call to produce a surah "from your own speech, as Muhammad brought it in your languages".[2]

Ismail al-Faruqi pointed out what kind of sign this is. The miracles of earlier prophets overwhelmed the senses; the Quran's sign is addressed to the mind of anyone who knows Arabic, and it stays open to inspection in every generation. A claim that the challenge has been met is therefore a claim about Arabic literature, and it can be tested.[3]

The "random Persian" of the post is not al-Ma'arri. Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri was born in 973 at Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in Syria and died there in 449 AH (1057), and his full name carries the tribal name al-Tanukhi: he belonged to the Arab tribe of Tanukh.[4]

He was one of the great poets of classical Arabic and a scholar of its grammar and rare vocabulary. He was also a sceptic about much of the religion around him, which is why his name comes up whenever a critic of Islam wants a witness from inside the tradition.[5]

The book's title means "Paragraphs and Endings". A study of it published in 2012 by Ali Kanjiyan Khanari, Abdolahad Ghaibi and Farshid Farajzadeh describes its plan: chapters arranged by the letters of the alphabet, short rhymed paragraphs, rare words and terms drawn from grammar, law, history and astronomy.[4]

The plan is a display of skill. Each of its twenty-eight chapters belongs to one letter of the alphabet, and the rhymes of that chapter end on it. In many passages al-Ma'arri also made the rhymes share two or more letters, a harder rule than custom required, the same discipline he imposed on his collection of poems Luzum ma la yalzam, "the necessity of what is not necessary".[4]

Its subject is the praise of God. The authors divide its content into two themes: the glorification of God by rational creatures and by the rest of creation. They quote Shawqi Dayf, the historian of Arabic literature: "this is a book that is all exhortation", written "to glorify God, the Most High".[4]

A 2024 study of the book's language, by Jaafar Raham Jasim and Maytham Muhammad Ali, shows what kind of text it is. Al-Ma'arri glosses his own rare words in the book itself: in one passage he explains musawwiha and mulwiya, two words for a withered meadow. The study notes that, "as is his custom", he opens the passage by glorifying God.[6]

The charge that al-Ma'arri wrote the book "in opposition to the word of God" comes from his later biographers. The 2012 study names Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Dhahabi and Haji Khalifa, and it notes that some of them suspected the book because of its author's reputation for scepticism.[4]

The study adds the detail that gave the suspicion its edge: one form of the book's title reads al-Fusul wa al-Ghayat fi muhadhat al-suwar wa al-ayat, "in parallel with the surahs and verses". The word muhadhat means setting one thing alongside another, and the question is what the book sets alongside the Quran.[4]

Other scholars read it differently. Taha Husayn wrote: "I do not think Abu al-'Ala' ever thought of such a thing, for he was too humble to aspire to that rank, and too astute to undertake a work for which there is no way." Dayf answered the question of the title directly: al-Ma'arri meant to stand alongside the Quran in the praise of God, and his style was a means to that end.[4]

The study's own conclusion is careful. Al-Ma'arri imitated the Quran's rhyme in places, out of admiration: one passage follows the endings of Surat al-Shams and closes with its last verse, "and He fears not the consequence of it" (91:15). The Quranic style covers only parts of the book, and so, the authors conclude, the book was no attempt to rival the Quran.[4]

The orientalist R. A. Nicholson, in his Literary History of the Arabs, takes the other view. He presents al-Ma'arri as a sceptic who "could not altogether refrain from doubting if it was really the Word of God, but he thought so well of the style that he accepted the challenge". Al-Ma'arri, he writes, "accepted the challenge flung down by Muhammad and produced a rival work", which "appears to have been a somewhat frivolous parody of the sacred volume".[7]

Nicholson then adds the decisive detail: "in the author's judgment its inferiority was simply due to the fact that it was not yet polished by the tongues of four centuries of readers." On Nicholson's own account, the author of the "rival work" judged it inferior to the Quran.[7]

The post's argument therefore fails on either reading. If the 2012 study is right, al-Ma'arri never made the attempt. If Nicholson is right, he made it and conceded it fell short, and nearly a thousand years of readers have given his book no place beside the Quran.

The True Furqan appeared in the United States in 1999, published by WinePress Publishing of Enumclaw, Washington. It is credited to two pseudonymous authors, "Al Saffee" and "Al Mahdee", with an English translation by the evangelist Anis Shorrosh, and it runs to seventy-seven numbered chapters in Arabic and English.[8]

It borrows the Quran's form, its rhymed endings, its openings and much of its vocabulary, to preach Christian doctrine, the Trinity included. Its own makers presented it as a missionary book addressed to Muslims.[8]

The book's translator presented it as an answer to the Quran's challenge. On the commentators' reading of the challenge, the answer fails on its own terms: "like it" meant like the Quran "in truth and truthfulness", and a text written to preach what the Quran denies has chosen to differ from it at the very point the challenge names. A critic who rejects that standard can still apply the plainer one, the judgement of those who know Arabic.

A text built from the Quran's own phrases and rhythms has taken its standard from the book it claims to answer. The challenge asks for a composition that stands beside the Quran in the judgement of those who know Arabic; a quarter of a century later, no school of Arabic letters or community of readers treats The True Furqan as that equal.

Attempts at a rival are as old as the challenge. The sayings of Musaylima, the claimant to prophecy in Yamama, were remembered by the early historians, and remembered as a failure; we set out that record in our article on the Hanif poets and Musaylima.[9]

Each attempt confirms what the challenge assumes: the Quran can be imitated in rhyme and phrase, and the imitation is recognised as an imitation. The test is whether the result is received as an equal, and the two books in the post have not been. The challenge has even outlived its most gifted sceptic: al-Ma'arri, who doubted that the Quran came from God, still judged his own composition below it, by Nicholson's account, and asked for four centuries of recitation to close the gap.

A critic remains free to argue that the Quran is a human work. The case has to be made from the Quran itself, and our articles on who wrote the Quran and on the claim of grammatical errors in the Quran take up the arguments that try.

The bottom line

Al-Ma'arri was an Arab of Tanukh, and his al-Fusul wa al-Ghayat is a book of exhortation in praise of God. One modern study holds that he never meant it as a rival. Nicholson holds that he did, and reports that the author himself judged it inferior.

The True Furqan is a missionary pastiche of 1999, built from the Quran's own form and vocabulary to carry a Christian message. Neither book has been received as the Quran's equal by those who know the language, and that reception is the test the challenge sets. God knows best.

Notes

  3. Ismail R. al Faruqi, Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (Kuala Lumpur: Muslim Youth Movement of Malaysia, 1983), III.D, on i'jaz and the contrast with the miracles of earlier prophets.
  4. The edition they use is al-Ma'arri, al-Fusul wa al-Ghayat, edited by Mahmud Hasan Zanati (Cairo: al-Hay'a al-Misriyya al-'Amma). The article gives al-Ma'arri's full name, his birthplace and his death in Rabi' al-Awwal 449.
  5. R. A. Nicholson, A Literary History of the Arabs (London: T. Fisher Unwin, 1907), p. 318.
  6. Mahmud Hasan Zanati (Cairo, 1938), p. 36. On the book's reception, see also Devin J. Stewart, "Rhythmical Anxiety: Notes on Abu l-'Ala al-Ma'arri's (d. 449/1058) al-Fusul wa'l-Ghayat and Its Reception", in Nuha Alshaar (ed.), The Qur'an and Adab: The Shaping of Literary Traditions in Classical Islam (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2017), pp. 239–272.
  7. R. A. Nicholson, A Literary History of the Arabs (London: T. Fisher Unwin, 1907), p. 318.
  8. Al Saffee and Al Mahdee, The True Furqan: Al-Furqan al-Haqq, translated by Anis Shorrosh (Enumclaw: WinePress Publishing, 1999).
  9. Al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk, the accounts of Musaylima and the battle of Yamama.
